text: Table 2 distinguishes coverage recovery through calibration weighting from interval shortening through fitting, at a 90% target. On ordered electricity data, keeping least squares fixed while weighting calibration residuals raises temporal-average coverage from 85.2% to 89.0%, but increases mean width from 0.565 to 0.606. With calibration weighting retained, weighted least squares gives 89.3% coverage and width 0.527: narrower intervals accompany slightly higher observed coverage, although both weighted methods remain below target. The randomly permuted, exchangeable version of the same data changes that comparison. Unweighted least squares, residual-weighted least squares, and residual-weighted weighted least squares attain 89.9%, 90.8%, and 90.8% coverage, with widths 0.639, 0.652, and 0.663, respectively. Thus weighted fitting provides no width advantage in the control, and weighting increases variability. These averages support complementary calibration and fitting roles on ordered data, not coverage at every prediction time. Arbitrary drift can produce a large weighted total-variation penalty between original and swapped residual distributions; the empirical gains therefore do not establish universal 90% coverage.

Table 2 separates improved coverage from narrower intervals in electricity-transfer prediction. In the original time order, unweighted full conformal with least squares yields 85.2% coverage and mean width 0.565. Keeping least squares but weighting calibration residuals raises coverage to 89.0% while increasing width to 0.606; adding weighted least-squares fitting gives 89.3% and width 0.527. Thus calibration weighting moves coverage toward the 90% target at a width cost, whereas weighted fitting produces narrower intervals with similar coverage in this setting. Neither weighted method reaches the target. In the randomly permuted, exchangeable control, these three methods have coverage 89.9%, 90.8%, and 90.8%, with widths 0.639, 0.652, and 0.663, respectively. The weighted-fitting width advantage does not persist after random permutation. These time-averaged comparisons neither establish coverage at every time point nor guarantee 90% coverage under arbitrary drift. For the randomized construction, a near-nominal coverage lower bound requires a small weighted swapped-residual total-variation term.

Unequal calibration weights and order-sensitive fitting obstruct the usual exchangeable-residual argument. Theorem 2b prespecifies weights w_i in [0,1] and algorithm tags t_i, normalizes the weights with unit test weight, and draws K independently of the data using these probabilities. Swap observation K with the test point before fitting, retaining positional tags; at the true test label, the test residual occupies position K in the swapped residual vector. Residuals above the swapped vector's weighted (1-alpha)-quantile carry total normalized weight at most alpha. The rejection test is unchanged if its threshold places the test weight at infinity; because w_i <= 1, this threshold dominates the swapped-vector quantile. Miscoverage thus requires K to be a high-residual index. Independence permits averaging over K. Comparing each swapped residual law with the original adds its total-variation distance; the original-law weighted mass is at most alpha. Miscoverage is consequently bounded by alpha plus the weighted distances.

Full conformal prediction ordinarily relies on exchangeable data and symmetric fitting. We extend it with fixed calibration weights in [0,1], fixed algorithm tags, and a data-independent weighted random swap. Weights emphasize observations expected to resemble the test distribution; tags enable order-sensitive fitting. The swap connects miscoverage to high-residual indices, whose total normalized weight is at most alpha for any residual vector. Comparing original and swapped residual-vector distributions then gives finite-sample coverage at least 1 - alpha minus their weighted total-variation discrepancy. Under exchangeability this penalty vanishes, restoring nominal validity even with nonsymmetric fitting; otherwise, a small penalty limits undercoverage. When residuals are distinct, small discrepancy and normalized test weight also limit overcoverage. Related bounds cover split conformal and jackknife+, the latter with baseline 1 - 2 alpha. In simulations and electricity data, calibration weighting improves coverage, whereas weighted least-squares fitting can narrow intervals. On ordered electricity data, calibration weighting raises coverage from 85.2% to 89.0% but widens intervals; adding weighted fitting yields 89.3% coverage and narrower intervals. Both remain below the 90% target, and the width advantage disappears under random permutation. Election-data improvements also remain below target.

Nonexchangeable observations and order-sensitive model fitting break the usual symmetry argument for full conformal coverage. We extend split and full conformal prediction and jackknife+ by separating calibration weighting from tagged model fitting. Prespecified calibration weights in [0,1] emphasize observations believed comparable to the test point, while fixed tags let fitting exploit order. For full conformal prediction, a data-independent swap exchanges the test observation with an index sampled using normalized calibration weights and unit test weight before fitting. The swap links miscoverage to high-residual indices whose weighted mass cannot exceed alpha, without requiring symmetric fitting. Coverage is therefore at least 1-alpha minus a weighted sum of total-variation distances between original and swapped residual distributions; jackknife+ instead starts from 1-2alpha. Exchangeability eliminates this penalty, preserving validity. Under nonexchangeability, a small penalty limits undercoverage; distinct residuals and a small normalized test weight also limit overcoverage. Nonexchangeable simulations and ordered electricity data support complementary roles: calibration weighting improves coverage but widens intervals, whereas weighted fitting can shorten them. That width advantage disappears in the exchangeable, randomly permuted electricity control. Election coverage improves but remains below 90%, underscoring that arbitrary drift is not covered by a nominal guarantee.

Unlike symmetric fitting, nonsymmetric fitting need not produce exchangeable residuals. Prespecify calibration weights w_i in [0,1] and fixed tags; normalize by D = 1 + sum_i w_i, giving the test point weight 1/D. Draw K independently using these weights and swap observation K with the candidate test observation, keeping tags at their positions. At the true response, miscoverage implies that the test residual, now at index K, exceeds the swapped vector's weighted (1 - alpha)-quantile. The implication follows by replacing the test residual by infinity in the quantile and noting that each calibration weight is at most the test weight. For every residual vector, these high-residual indices carry normalized mass at most alpha. Independence allows averaging over K; comparing each swapped-vector event with its original-vector counterpart adds at most their total-variation distance. Hence miscoverage is bounded by alpha plus the weighted residual-distribution discrepancy, without algorithm symmetry or stability.
